title: Reliability Engineering
summary: Reliability engineering is the discipline of building systems that work correctly under adversity—hardware failures, software bugs, network issues, traffic spikes, and human error. It encompasses fault tolerance patterns, failure mode analysis, operational practices, and the cultural shift from reactive firefighting to proactive resilience. Understanding availability math, failure patterns, and resilience techniques is essential for designing systems that meet production SLAs.

sections.title: Availability Math: Nines and Error Budgets
paragraphs: Availability is expressed as the percentage of time a system is operational: 99% (two nines) = 87.6 hours downtime/year; 99.9% (three nines) = 8.76 hours; 99.99% (four nines) = 52.6 minutes; 99.999% (five nines) = 5.26 minutes. Each additional nine reduces allowable downtime by 10x. The jump from three to four nines (from 8.76 hours to 52.6 minutes annual downtime) requires dramatically different architecture—you cannot achieve four nines with manual deployments or single-node databases.

Serial dependencies multiply availability downward. If your service depends on three services each with 99.9% availability, your composite availability is 0.999^3 = 99.7%. Adding more dependencies makes the system less reliable, even if each dependency is individually reliable. This is why microservice architectures must implement bulkheads and circuit breakers to prevent dependency unavailability from cascading to the calling service. For high availability, minimize the number of synchronous dependencies in the critical path.

Error budget is the operationalized form of an SLA. If your SLO is 99.9% uptime, your error budget is 0.1% = 43.8 minutes/month. Incidents consume error budget. When the error budget is exhausted, development velocity should slow (fewer risky deployments) and reliability work should take priority. When error budget is ample, teams can move fast. This contractual relationship between reliability and velocity is the core of the SRE model.
bullets: Serial dependencies: 3 × 99.9% services = 99.7% composite availability
Error budget = 1 - SLO; when exhausted, slow velocity and prioritize reliability work
Four nines requires automated deployments, multi-AZ, and automatic failover

sections.title: Fault Tolerance Patterns: Redundancy and Failover
paragraphs: Redundancy is the fundamental mechanism of fault tolerance. Active-passive: one primary handles all traffic; a standby waits to take over on failure. Failover time (the time to detect failure and redirect traffic) is typically 30–120 seconds for database failover. Active-active: multiple instances handle traffic simultaneously; loss of one reduces capacity but does not stop service. Active-active requires that all instances can handle any request (stateless application tiers) or that requests are routed appropriately (each database shard has an active-active pair).

Geographic redundancy is essential for the highest availability targets. A single-region active-active system can tolerate any single instance failure but is vulnerable to regional outages (AWS us-east-1 outage, Nov 2021 took down Reddit, Twitch, and thousands of other services). Multi-region active-active requires globally distributed traffic routing (Anycast or GeoDNS), data replication between regions (synchronous for strong consistency, asynchronous for lower latency), and careful handling of cross-region write conflicts.

Bulkheads (from ship design: compartments that prevent water from flooding the whole ship) isolate failures to a subset of capacity. Thread pool isolation: each downstream dependency gets its own thread pool; a slow dependency exhausts its own pool without affecting calls to other dependencies. Process isolation: separate processes or containers per tenant or per feature; a noisy tenant doesn't degrade others. Connection pool isolation: separate database connection pools per read vs write operations; a runaway long-running query doesn't block fast transactional queries.
bullets: Active-passive: fast failover but underutilizes standby; 30–120s typical DB failover time
Active-active: no failover; instant capacity reduction on node loss; requires stateless or routed requests
Multi-region: tolerates regional outages; requires GeoDNS/Anycast + cross-region replication
Bulkhead: isolate failures; separate thread pools/connection pools per dependency or tenant

sections.title: Circuit Breakers, Retries, and Timeouts
paragraphs: A timeout is the simplest reliability pattern: don't wait forever for a response. Set a timeout on every network call. Without timeouts, a slow dependency causes your service to accumulate threads/connections waiting for responses, eventually exhausting your resource pool and causing your service to fail—even though the dependency is 'just slow,' not 'completely down.' Rules of thumb: set timeout to p99 latency × 2–3x for a buffer; always set timeouts on database queries (even SELECT queries can run for minutes if they encounter a table scan).

Circuit breaker pattern (Michael Nygard, Release It!): tracks recent failures; when failure rate exceeds a threshold, 'trips' the breaker to OPEN state; in OPEN state, calls fail immediately without reaching the dependency (fast failure). After a timeout, transitions to HALF-OPEN: a single probe request tests if the dependency has recovered. If it succeeds, the breaker CLOSES; if it fails, stays OPEN. This pattern converts long-timeout-cascade into fast-fail-cascade, dramatically reducing blast radius when a dependency fails.

Retries require careful policy design. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter: first retry after 1s, second after 2s+jitter, third after 4s+jitter—caps at some maximum. Respect Retry-After headers from 429 and 503 responses. Max retries: 3–5 is typical; more than 5 risks holding connections too long. Never retry non-idempotent operations (POST payment) without idempotency keys. Never retry on 4xx errors (client errors; retrying doesn't help). Always retry on network errors and 5xx (server errors; they may be transient).
bullets: Timeout: set on every network call; without it, slow dependency exhausts your resource pool
Circuit breaker: CLOSED → OPEN (on failure threshold) → HALF-OPEN (probe) → CLOSED (on success)
Retry: exponential backoff + jitter; max 3–5 retries; never retry non-idempotent without idempotency key
Retry budget: limit total retries across all clients; prevent retry storms on recovering service

sections.title: Graceful Degradation and Load Shedding
paragraphs: Graceful degradation means providing reduced but functional service when a dependency is unavailable. A product page that cannot load reviews should still show the product details and 'Add to Cart' button—not a 500 error. A search results page that cannot fetch personalization data should show generic results—not fail completely. Design every feature with a degraded fallback: cached data, default values, simplified response, or omitted non-critical sections. Chaos engineering (injecting failures in production) tests whether graceful degradation works as intended.

Load shedding actively rejects low-priority requests when the system is overloaded. As CPU, memory, or queue depth approaches a threshold, start rejecting requests with 503 Service Unavailable. Prioritize by user tier (premium users served before free tier), request type (checkout ahead of browsing), or recency (new requests ahead of old ones in queue). Load shedding prevents a traffic spike from causing complete service failure; instead, some requests are rejected cleanly, and the system continues serving capacity-proportional traffic.

Health checks are the operational backbone of reliability. Liveness checks determine if the process should be restarted (failed = restart the container). Readiness checks determine if the process should receive traffic (failed = remove from load balancer pool). Startup probes handle slow-starting containers that need longer to become ready. Kubernetes uses all three. The critical mistake: liveness check that depends on an external service—a database outage causes all pods to restart in a loop, amplifying the incident. Liveness checks must only test the process's own health.
bullets: Graceful degradation: return cached/default data when dependency fails; never fail completely
Load shedding: reject low-priority requests at threshold; prioritize critical operations
Liveness check: is this process healthy? Failed = restart. Only check process-local state.
Readiness check: can this process serve traffic? Failed = remove from load balancer pool.

sections.title: Failure Mode Analysis: FMEA and Game Days
paragraphs: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) systematically identifies what can fail in a system and what the impact would be. For each component, ask: what happens if this component fails completely? What if it's slow (latency spike)? What if it returns incorrect results (silent corruption)? The answers reveal which failures are tolerable (a non-critical analytics service slow = acceptable), which degrade gracefully (cache miss = fallback to DB), and which are catastrophic (payment DB fails = complete service outage). FMEA should be done before launch and after each significant architecture change.

Game days (or DiRT exercises—Disaster Recovery Testing) are planned exercises where failures are intentionally injected to test whether the system and team respond correctly. Shut down a database replica; block traffic to one availability zone; inject latency into a critical dependency. Game days reveal: gaps in monitoring (the team doesn't know something failed until a customer reports it), gaps in runbooks (the incident response procedure is missing a step), and gaps in architecture (graceful degradation never actually degrades gracefully under real failure conditions). Game days are the precursor to full chaos engineering.

Chaos engineering (Netflix Chaos Monkey) continuously and randomly terminates instances in production to verify that the system tolerates individual instance failures. The key principle: run chaos experiments in production, not just staging, because production has real traffic patterns, real data sizes, and real dependencies that staging cannot replicate. Start with the smallest possible blast radius (kill one instance during low-traffic periods with an on-call engineer watching) and expand scope as confidence grows.
bullets: FMEA: for each component, what happens on complete failure / slowness / incorrect results?
Game day: planned failure injection; tests monitoring, runbooks, and actual degradation behavior
Chaos engineering: continuous random failure injection in production; starts small, expands with confidence
Key question for every dependency: what happens to my service if this is down for 1 minute? 1 hour?

deepDive.title: Cascading Failures and Prevention
paragraphs: Cascading failures occur when a partial failure causes load to redistribute to remaining capacity, which then fails under increased load, causing further redistribution. Example: 1 of 3 database replicas fails; remaining 2 each handle 50% more load; they begin to slow down; slower responses cause clients to hold connections longer; connection pool exhausts; service fails. The cascade transforms a 33% capacity loss into a complete outage.

Prevention mechanisms: (1) Reject excess load (load shedding) before replicas are overloaded. (2) Circuit breakers prevent avalanche by fast-failing to overloaded dependencies. (3) Admission control queues requests and enforces concurrency limits (a web server that accepts unlimited concurrent requests in-flight will page-fault and OOM under spike; concurrency limits prevent this). (4) Autoscaling to add capacity when load increases. (5) Backpressure from downstream propagated upstream to slow producers.

Retry storms are a form of cascading failure: when a service starts failing, all clients simultaneously start retrying, multiplying the load on the struggling service. Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries over time. Retry budgets (maximum total retries across all clients, enforced by a token bucket in the proxy) cap the total retry amplification. Circuit breakers in clients stop retrying when the breaker is open.

deepDive.title: Reliability in Deployment
paragraphs: Canary deployments reduce blast radius of new code: deploy to 1% of traffic first, observe error rates and latency for 30–60 minutes, then progressively roll to 10%, 50%, 100%. Automated rollback triggers when error rate or latency exceeds threshold during canary. This is not just best practice—at scale, it is the only way to deploy new code safely (100% deployments have caused catastrophic failures at every major tech company).

Feature flags decouple deployment from release. Code is deployed to all instances but runs behind a flag (disabled). The flag is enabled for 1% of users, then 10%, then 100%—independently of the deployment cadence. This allows hot-rollback: if the feature causes problems, disable the flag without redeployment. Feature flags are the operational equivalent of circuit breakers for new features.

expert.title: Expert: Tail Latency and the 99th Percentile
paragraphs: High p99 latency is often more damaging than high p50 latency because it affects a consistent subset of users (those who happen to be served by a loaded shard, a GC-pausing JVM, or a cold cache). Hedged requests (send the same request to two replicas, use the first response, cancel the second) reduce p99 latency at the cost of double the resource usage. Google's Spanner uses hedged reads extensively; the overhead is acceptable because it brings p99 much closer to p50.

Coordinated omission is a measurement fallacy: when benchmarking a system by sending 1000 requests, if request 500 is slow (100ms instead of 1ms), subsequent requests are queued and also measured as slow—even though the system would have processed them normally if the benchmark hadn't queued them. Tools like wrk2 and HDR Histogram correct for coordinated omission by tracking scheduled vs actual send times and attributing excess latency to the right percentile.

Deploy circuit breakers at every external service call boundary; tune open threshold carefully
Implement graceful degradation fallbacks for every external dependency
Use canary deployments (1% → 10% → 50% → 100%) with automated rollback on error rate threshold
Conduct FMEA before launch; run game days quarterly to test runbooks and monitoring

Liveness check depending on database: DB outage causes all pods to restart in a loop
Cascading failure from no load shedding: spike on 2 of 3 replicas means remaining 1 gets all traffic
Retry storms: all clients simultaneously retry a recovering service, overwhelming it again
Active-passive failover without automated testing: manual failover procedure has never been practiced

examples.title: Netflix Chaos Monkey
examples.description: Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminates EC2 instances in production during business hours. When introduced, it immediately revealed that many services did not gracefully handle instance failures. Teams were forced to implement proper retry logic, fallbacks, and health checks to survive Chaos Monkey. The result: Netflix's services are significantly more resilient than before Chaos Monkey, and the team can be confident that surviving a random instance failure is a baseline property of all services.

examples.title: AWS Route 53 Multi-Region Active-Active
examples.description: A global SaaS platform serves users from three AWS regions (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) using Route 53 latency routing. Each region has an independent stack with asynchronous cross-region replication for the database. When us-east-1 had a partial outage, Route 53 health checks detected degraded health, shifted traffic to eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1 within 60 seconds, and maintained 99.99% availability during the incident—even though one region was substantially impaired.

keyTakeaways: Every additional nine of availability requires 10x more architectural rigor; plan accordingly
Serial dependency chains multiply downward: minimize synchronous critical-path dependencies
Circuit breakers + timeouts + retries form the standard resilience stack for every network call
Graceful degradation is a design discipline: plan fallbacks for every external dependency
FMEA + game days + chaos engineering form a progression of reliability validation maturity
Error budgets make the velocity-reliability trade-off explicit and policy-driven
whyItMatters: Reliability is the product reliability of every downstream component. Without explicit reliability design—fault tolerance patterns, failure mode analysis, operational practices—production systems inevitably experience cascading failures, extended outages, and customer impact. Senior engineers are expected to reason about failure modes and design resilient systems; reliability engineering is the structured approach to that reasoning.
reflectionQuestions: Your service depends on 5 downstream services each with 99.9% availability. What is your composite availability, and how can you improve it?
Design the circuit breaker configuration for a payment service calling an external payment processor. What thresholds do you use?
A cascading failure takes down your entire API within 2 minutes of a database replica failure. Walk through the failure mode and propose three architectural changes to prevent it.
You have a 99.99% SLO. How much error budget do you have per month, and what does that mean for your deployment frequency?
numbersToKnow: Active-passive DB failover: 30–120 seconds typical; active-active: 0 seconds (capacity reduction only)
Circuit breaker: typical open threshold 50% error rate over 10-second window
Canary deployment: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%; each stage held for 30–60min observation
